title: Quality improvement and clinical audit
blurb: Use the Model for Improvement, PDSA cycles and the audit cycle, and tell audit apart from service evaluation and research.
question: A ward's audit shows that only 70% of patients have a falls assessment within 24 hours, against a trust standard of 95%. The team introduces an admission checklist. What should happen next?

teach.body: Quality improvement (QI) is a systematic way of making care safer, more effective and more person-centred by testing changes and measuring whether they help. Clinical audit is one QI tool: it measures care against agreed standards and acts to bring practice in line with them (HQIP). In plain English: QI asks 'can we do this better?'; audit asks 'are we doing what we said we would?'. Every nurse evaluates care and uses audit findings to improve (proficiencies P6.4 and P6.7).
teach.cite: HQIP; NHS England QSIR; proficiency P6.4, P6.7

teach.h: The Model for Improvement: three questions
head: Question
It defines
rows: What are we trying to accomplish?
How will we know a change is an improvement?
What change can we make that will result in improvement?
teach.caption: Ideas are then tested in rapid Plan, Do, Study, Act (PDSA) cycles.

steps.label: Do
steps.sub: run the small test, collect data

teach.caption: Start small (one patient, one shift), then build up as confidence grows.
Re-audit against the same standard shows whether the change worked and has been sustained.

head: Measure
Tells you
Example (falls project)
rows: Whether the system works as planned
Whether the change causes problems elsewhere
teach.caption: NHS England QSIR, Measuring quality care. Structure measures (staff, equipment) are sometimes added.

teach.h: Improve with people, not to them
teach.body: Proficiency P6.9 asks nurses to work with people, their families and colleagues to develop improvement strategies, sharing feedback and learning. That means co-designing changes with people who use the service, asking for their experience, and feeding back results. P5.10 adds contributing to supervision and team reflection: regular team discussion of what went well and what could change turns everyday experience into improvement.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Charge Nurse Ben on a surgical ward
teach.body: Ben's audit shows 70% of patients had a falls assessment within 24 hours against a 95% standard. His team's aim: 95% within three months. They test an admission checklist with two nurses for one week (Plan, Do), find it takes too long (Study), shorten it (Act) and spread it. Process measure: % assessed in 24 hours; outcome: falls rate; balancing: time taken to admit. After three months they re-audit against the same standard and share the results with staff and the patient panel.
teach.cite: HQIP audit cycle; NHS England Model for Improvement

teach.text: The S in PDSA is STUDY (analyse and compare with the prediction), not 'Check'. And audit measures against a standard; research creates new generalisable knowledge and normally needs NHS research ethics review.

items: Model for Improvement: aim, measures, change ideas; test with PDSA cycles, starting small.
Audit cycle: standard, measure, compare, change, re-audit.
Audit uses a standard; service evaluation describes current care; research generates new knowledge.
Outcome, process and balancing measures together show whether change helps without harm elsewhere.
Co-design improvement with people and families and share learning through team reflection.

summary: You can now plan an improvement using the Model for Improvement and PDSA cycles, run and close an audit cycle, and choose outcome, process and balancing measures. You can also distinguish audit from service evaluation and research and involve people and families in improvement.

A.q: In a PDSA cycle, which stage involves analysing the data and comparing the results with what was predicted?
options: Plan
Do
Study
Act
A.why: Plan sets the objective and predictions, Do runs the test and collects data, Study analyses the results against the predictions, and Act decides whether to adopt, adapt or abandon the change (NHS England PDSA guidance).

whyNot.0: Plan sets the aim, prediction and arrangements before the test.
whyNot.1: Do carries out the test and collects data, without the analysis.
whyNot.3: Act uses what was learnt in Study to adopt, adapt or abandon the change.

A.q: A team checks how many patients had their VTE assessment recorded within 14 hours, against the trust policy standard. What type of project is this?
options: Research, as it collects patient data
Service evaluation, as it describes the current care
Clinical audit, as it measures against standards
A PDSA test of a new change idea
A.why: Clinical audit measures current practice against an agreed standard and acts to bring practice in line (HQIP; HRA Defining Research table).

whyNot.0: Research seeks new generalisable knowledge; collecting data against a local standard is audit.
whyNot.1: Service evaluation describes current care without a standard; here there is a policy standard.
whyNot.3: No change is being tested; existing practice is being measured.

A.q: A team using the Model for Improvement starts by agreeing what they want to achieve. Which question does this answer?
options: How will we know a change is an improvement?
What change can we make that will result in improvement?
Who is responsible for the problem?
What are we trying to accomplish?
A.why: The Model for Improvement asks: What are we trying to accomplish? (the aim); How will we know that a change is an improvement? (measures); What change can we make that will result in improvement? (change ideas).

whyNot.0: This question defines the measures, not the aim.
whyNot.1: This question generates change ideas, after the aim is set.
whyNot.2: Assigning responsibility is not one of the three questions; QI focuses on systems.

B.q: An audit found 70% compliance against a 95% standard. The team has trained staff and introduced a checklist. What is the next step in the audit cycle?
options: Publish the 70% result as the final result
Lower the standard to 80%
Re-audit against the same standard
Start a research study instead
B.why: The audit cycle is: agree the standard, measure, compare, implement change, then re-audit to see whether practice has improved and the change is sustained (HQIP).

whyNot.0: Publishing the first result without re-measuring leaves the loop open.
whyNot.1: Lowering the standard hides the gap instead of improving care.
whyNot.3: The question is whether practice now meets a standard, which re-audit answers.

B.q: A nurse wants to randomly allocate patients to two dressing types to find out which heals wounds faster, and publish the results. What does this require?
options: Research ethics committee review
Approval from the ward manager as an audit
Registration as a service evaluation
A PDSA cycle on one ward
B.why: Randomly allocating treatments to generate new, generalisable knowledge is research, which normally needs NHS research ethics committee review (HRA Defining Research table, 2022).

whyNot.1: This is not audit: there is no standard and treatment is allocated by the study.
whyNot.2: Service evaluation describes current care; it does not randomise treatments.
whyNot.3: A PDSA cycle tests a local change; randomising patients to compare treatments is research.

B.q: A ward's project aims to get patients walking sooner after surgery. Which is the best balancing measure?
options: Number of patients walking on day 1
Average length of stay after surgery
Patient satisfaction with mobility
Number of falls on the ward
B.why: Balancing measures check whether improving one part of a system causes problems elsewhere. Earlier walking could increase falls, so the falls rate is a balancing measure (NHS England QSIR).

whyNot.0: Patients walking on day 1 shows whether the process is happening: a process measure.
whyNot.1: Length of stay reflects the impact of the change on patients: an outcome measure.
whyNot.2: Satisfaction with mobility is an outcome of the change, not a check for harm elsewhere.

C.q: A community team wants to find out how long people currently wait for a first visit after referral. There is no agreed standard. What type of project is this?
options: Clinical audit
Service evaluation
Research
A PDSA cycle
C.why: Service evaluation measures current care without reference to a standard; audit requires a standard and research seeks generalisable new knowledge (HRA Defining Research table, 2022).

whyNot.0: Audit needs an agreed standard to measure against, and there is none.
whyNot.2: The team is describing its own current service, not creating generalisable knowledge.
whyNot.3: No change is being tested; the team is measuring current performance.

C.q: Priya designs a new handover sheet and wants to introduce it across the whole hospital next month. What is the best advice using the Model for Improvement?
options: Launch it hospital-wide to get the most data
Test it on one shift, measure, adapt and then spread
Wait for a national template before changing anything
Ask each ward to design its own sheet instead
C.why: The Model for Improvement uses rapid, small-scale PDSA cycles: test a change on a small scale, measure the effect, adapt, and build up once it works. This limits risk and builds learning and ownership (NHS England).

whyNot.0: A large untested launch risks widespread problems and gives less useful learning.
whyNot.2: Local improvement does not need to wait for a national template.
whyNot.3: Abandoning the idea for many separate versions loses the chance to test and learn.

C.q: A diabetes team wants to improve the information given to people newly diagnosed. Which approach best reflects proficiency P6.9?
options: Copy a leaflet another trust uses for adults
Ask the consultant to rewrite the existing leaflet
Use the lowest-cost printing option available
Co-design it with people recently diagnosed
C.why: P6.9 asks nurses to work with people, families and colleagues to develop improvement strategies. Co-design with people who have lived experience makes information relevant and accessible.

whyNot.0: Copying another trust's leaflet does not involve local people's needs or feedback.
whyNot.1: A professional-only rewrite misses the experience of the people who use the information.
whyNot.2: Cost matters, but it does not improve the quality or relevance of the information.

reteach.title: Recipe testing
reteach.question: How would you improve a family recipe without ruining Sunday lunch?

blocks.body: You decide what 'better' means (the aim), how you will taste it (the measures), and what to try (the change). You test one tweak on a small batch (Plan, Do), taste it honestly against your prediction (Study), and keep, adjust or drop it (Act). Audit is different: it checks whether you followed the recipe you agreed (the standard), fixes what is wrong, then checks again.

blocks.text: An audit without re-audit is an unfinished audit: you do not know whether your change worked.

explain.body: Aim: what are we trying to accomplish? Measures: how will we know a change is an improvement? Changes: what change can we make that will result in improvement?

test.q: Which Model for Improvement question is answered by choosing outcome, process and balancing measures?
options: What are we trying to accomplish here?
What change can we make that will result in improvement?
How will we know a change is an improvement?
Who will lead and manage the project?
test.why: 'How will we know that a change is an improvement?' is answered by selecting measures (NHS England Model for Improvement; QSIR).

whyNot.3: Leadership is important but is not one of the three questions.

explain.body: Plan the test and predict the result; Do it on a small scale and collect data; Study the results against the prediction; Act: adopt, adapt or abandon, then plan the next cycle.

test.q: After studying the results of a small test, a team decides to adjust the change and test it again. Which PDSA stage is this?
options: Plan
Do
Study
Act
test.why: In Act the team decides to adopt, adapt or abandon the change based on what was learnt, leading into the next cycle (NHS England PDSA guidance).

whyNot.0: Plan prepares the next test once the Act decision has been made.
whyNot.2: Study analyses the data; the decision to adapt comes in Act.

explain.body: Agree the standard, measure practice, compare with the standard, make changes, then re-audit against the same standard.

test.q: What does re-audit add to the clinical audit cycle?
options: It sets the standard for the very first time
It shows if the changes improved practice
It turns the audit into a research study
It replaces the need to make any changes
test.why: Re-audit measures practice again against the same standard after changes, showing whether improvement has happened and been sustained (HQIP).

whyNot.0: The standard is agreed at the start of the cycle.
whyNot.2: Re-audit is still audit; it does not generate generalisable knowledge.
whyNot.3: Re-audit follows changes; it does not replace them.

explain.body: Audit measures against a standard. Service evaluation measures current care without a standard. Research seeks new generalisable knowledge and normally needs NHS research ethics committee review.

test.q: Which project normally needs review by an NHS research ethics committee?
options: A trial randomising patients to two dressings
An audit of hand hygiene against trust policy
A survey of the current clinic waiting times
A PDSA test of a new handover sheet
test.why: Research, such as a trial randomising patients to treatments, normally needs NHS REC review; audit and service evaluation do not (HRA Defining Research table, 2022).

whyNot.1: Audit against policy does not normally need REC review.
whyNot.2: Describing current waiting times is service evaluation.
whyNot.3: A local PDSA test is improvement work, not research.
